extracted.subtask_description: Comprehensive encyclopedic guidance on policy, clinical, regulatory, and harm-reduction standards for responding to the opioid epidemic, including prescribing guidelines, treatment program requirements, legal interventions, and community-level harm-reduction measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: CDC guideline for prescribing opioids (2016)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend opioids only be used when benefits for pain and function are expected to outweigh risks, and then used at the lowest effective dosage, with avoidance of concurrent opioid and benzodiazepine use whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guideline offers many non-pharmacological options as alternatives to prescribing opioids (example: physical therapist interventions). It is framed as a clinical standard intended to reduce inappropriate opioid prescribing and consequent harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) use
rubrics_metrics.description: PDMPs allow pharmacists and prescribers to access patients' prescription histories to identify suspicious use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of April 2017 PDMPs existed in every state. Physician uptake varies (2015 survey: 53% used PDMPs, 22% unaware). Implementation of PDMPs and pill-mill laws (e.g., Florida) led to large declines in opioid prescriptions by high-risk prescribers.

rubrics_metrics.name: AMA Opioid Task Force recommended physician actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Six actions for physicians: register and use state PDMPs; enhance education and training; support comprehensive treatment for pain and substance use disorders; help end stigma; co-prescribe naloxone to patients at risk of overdose; encourage safe storage and disposal of opioids and all medications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Task Force's progress report cites reductions in opioid prescriptions (22.2% decrease 2013–2017), increased physician participation in PDMPs (389% increase reported), and sharp increases in naloxone prescriptions and buprenorphine certification. These actions are presented as a multi-pronged clinician standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation and operational requirements for opioid treatment programs (OTPs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs are required to be accredited by SAMHSA or the Drug Enforcement Administration and must undergo a lengthy process including intensive training and site visit reviews; programs must submit to re-accreditation every 1–3 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These regulatory requirements are described as time- and resource-consuming and cited by GAO and others as barriers to expanding treatment capacity; accreditation status also determines ability to provide certain medications (e.g., buprenorphine in some contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Buprenorphine prescriber training and waiver; patient caps
rubrics_metrics.description: Office-based physicians who wish to prescribe buprenorphine for treatment of opioid use disorder must complete required training and apply for and receive a waiver from SAMHSA. Under regulation, physicians may not have more than 30 buprenorphine patients in their first year; they may apply to increase to 100 patients by year two and 275 patients by year three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a regulatory access criterion governing who may prescribe buprenorphine and at what patient volume; it shapes office-based access to medication-assisted treatment (MAT).

rubrics_metrics.name: SAMHSA training hours for buprenorphine administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Accredited programs are able to administer buprenorphine provided that those prescribing and administering the drug have completed the 8–24 hours of SAMHSA training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the training-hour requirement range for clinicians in accredited programs; ties training completion to program capacity to administer buprenorphine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission criteria for medication-assisted treatment (federal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal criteria for admission to treatment programs require potential patients to: have a diagnosable opioid use disorder according to the DSM-5; be actively addicted to opioids at the time of intake; and have been addicted to opioids for at least one year before beginning treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'high-threshold' federal admission criteria are cited by GAO as barriers to getting people into treatment; states may impose additional criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage and cost considerations for MAT
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicaid covers methadone treatments for low-income individuals but the extent of coverage depends on the state and on whether the state has opted into Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act; buprenorphine is often not covered and frequently must be paid for out-of-pocket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates disparities in access to lower-risk MAT (buprenorphine) versus higher-risk treatment for lower-income individuals; cost and insurance coverage are framed as practical access criteria affecting treatment uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-prescription and distribution of naloxone (take-home naloxone, THN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-prescribe naloxone to patients at risk of overdose; distribute take-home naloxone kits and provide naloxone training programs to communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: THN kits and community training have shown promise in reducing opioid overdose deaths, including in areas with increasing fentanyl availability. Evidence cited shows expanded naloxone access correlates with increased naloxone prescriptions and may not lead to riskier drug use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Samaritan Laws (GSLs) and Naloxone Access Laws (NALs) as bystander-intervention policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Two law types reduce opioid overdoses through increased bystander intervention: GSLs (protect bystanders from civil damages when providing emergency care) and NALs (increase naloxone distribution and accessibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most states have various degrees of naloxone access (third-party distribution, pharmacist prescribing, standing orders). Research indicates increases in NALs/GSLs are associated with reductions in overdose mortality (magnitudes and regional effects vary). Effectiveness depends on behavioral changes and naloxone accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naloxone access mechanisms (third-party distribution, pharmacist prescribing, standing orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most states provide naloxone access via three mechanisms: third-party distribution, pharmacist prescribing power, and standing orders; standing orders often allow distribution if a patient meets specific criteria (most often the prescription of an opioid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details the operational mechanisms by which naloxone can be made more widely available; notes standing orders' dependency on defined eligibility criteria and mixed evidence on effectiveness across regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Needle Exchange Programs (NEP) definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: NEPs (syringe services programs) are community-based programs that provide access to sterile needles and syringes free of cost and facilitate safe disposal of used needles and syringes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CDC and NIH cite NEPs as a vital part of a comprehensive response; evidence indicates NEPs do not increase drug use, increase admittance into addiction treatment centers, and help reduce public-health harms like discarded needles. Federal funding rules limiting NEPs were relaxed in early 2016 for certain program aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overdose prevention centers / safe injection sites (evidence and legal status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overdose prevention centers are supervised sites where people can inject under oversight; users at high risk express willingness to utilize them and they could reduce overdoses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of 2018, U.S. federal/state legislation generally did not allow such centers; critics argue they enable drug use while some data (2014) suggested they could reduce overdoses without increasing the number of users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and enforcement criteria for 'pill mills'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'pill mill' is a clinic that dispenses narcotics to patients without a legitimate medical purpose: characteristics include very quick patient exams, an office fee (e.g., $200–$400), very high patient throughput (up to ~60 patients/day), and large supply to black markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law enforcement and policy responses (pill mill statutes) have been used to close such operations (example: 250 pill mills shut down in Florida in 2015). Implementing pill mill laws and PDMPs reduced high-risk prescribing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homicide-by-overdose / drug-induced homicide (DIH) legal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Many states have 'homicide-by-overdose' or 'drug-induced homicide' laws allowing prosecutors to charge individuals who provide controlled substances that cause a death, including in cases that are unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws existed in about half of U.S. states as of 2019 and prosecutions increased substantially in the 21st century; legislatures in multiple states proposed enhancements to these laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative clinical standards for pharmacological MAT options (methadone vs. buprenorphine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methadone: long-acting synthetic opioid used since 1964, typically dispensed daily at clinics (though some jurisdictions allow take-homes), generally considered the 'gold standard' with evidence of reduced mortality. Buprenorphine: partial opioid agonist, considered safer and less regulated, can be prescribed in office settings with month-long prescriptions and has formulations like buprenorphine/naloxone and implants (Probuphine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry outlines relative advantages (methadone's evidence base and mortality reduction; buprenorphine's office-based access and lower regulatory burden) and access constraints (regulatory clinic requirements for methadone, training/waiver limits for buprenorphine). It also notes buprenorphine still carries some dependence risk and cost/coverage issues affect patient access.
